topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digit Emergence
target_audience: University students with a background in introductory physics (mechanics)

sections.title: The Hook: A Surprising Connection
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive phenomenon: counting the number of collisions between two blocks of different masses colliding elastically leads to the digits of Pi. Set the visual stage with a small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M = 100^n * m).
sections.example: Imagine a small mouse-sized block (m) colliding with an elephant-sized block (M) on a frictionless floor against a wall.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Review elastic collision principles: Conservation of Momentum (p = mv) and Conservation of Kinetic Energy (K = 1/2mv^2). Briefly represent these via vector arrows: m moving right, M stationary, and the resulting velocity swap/rebound.
sections.example: Use a visual 'velocity vector bar' that shrinks and expands as the blocks hit each other to illustrate energy transfer.

sections.title: Visualizing Phase Space
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Map the velocity of block m (v1) on the x-axis and the velocity of block M (v2) on the y-axis. Show that collisions are essentially reflections of the velocity vector against a boundary in this 2D plane.
sections.example: Visualize the state as a single point moving in a box; each collision is a 'bounce' against a line slanted at an angle determined by the square root of the mass ratio (sqrt(m/M)).

sections.title: The Geometric Bridge to Pi
sections.content: Explain that the total number of collisions is equivalent to the number of reflections in a wedge shaped by the angle θ = arctan(sqrt(m/M)). As M becomes much larger than m, the arc length of the trajectory approaches a circle's circumference divided by the angle.
sections.example: An animation showing a laser beam bouncing inside a V-shaped mirror where the number of bounces equals the digits of Pi.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Limit of Mass Ratios
sections.content: Summarize that as mass ratio M/m approaches 100^n, the collision count precisely reveals the first n+1 digits of Pi. Connect the physical 'chaos' of collisions to the deterministic nature of geometry.
sections.example: A final summary graphic showing the collision counter hitting 3, then 1, then 4, then 1, matching the digits of Pi as the large block grows exponentially.
